catalog_quote: [Vandermeiren 1913, p. 11] L'accent tonique joue un rôle important en kiluba hemba. En le déplaçant, on s'expose à ne pas être compris ou à dire des choses tout autres que celles qu'on voulait dire, car certains mots, en tout semblables pour l'orthographe, ont des sens totalement différents d'après la place qu'on donne à l'accent tonique. Bien plus, il arrive très souvent qu'un mot, écrit de la même manière et portant le même accent tonique, diffère, quant au sens, suivant que la voyelle de la syllabe est longue ou brève. L'usage certes devra être le guide le plus sûr; cependant, pour faciliter quelque peu le travail personnel, nous donnerons à chaque mot, autant que faire se peut, son accent tonique, soit au moyen d'un accent aigu pour l'a bref, l'e ouvert et bref, l'i bref, l'o bref et l'u bref; soit au moyen d'un accent grave pour l'a long, l'é fermé, l'i long, l'o grave et long et pour l'u long. [Colle 1913, II p. 661] Chaque mot comporte un accent, qui n'est pas l'accent prosodique, mais l'accent tonique, musical, ou aigu. Ces trois derniers mots désignent cette même inflexion élevée (le do aigu). Voici un mot de trois syllabes; il possède deux sons graves et un son aigu; le son aigu frappe soit la pénultième, soit l'antipénultième; on dira, par exemple: lùbuzi (une grande chèvre), bàluba, avec l'accent aigu sur lù et sur bà; ou bien kamùntu (un petit homme), avec l'accent aigu sur mù. Il en est de même des mots plus courts et plus longs.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: The tonic accent plays an important role in Kiluba Hemba. If one displaces it, one risks not being understood, or saying things quite different from what one meant, for certain words, wholly alike in spelling, have totally different meanings according to the place given to the tonic accent. What is more, it very often happens that a word written the same way and bearing the same tonic accent differs in meaning according to whether the vowel of the syllable is long or short. Usage will certainly have to be the surest guide; however, [...] we shall give each word, as far as possible, its tonic accent
new_statements.citation: Vandermeiren, Joseph (1913). Vocabulaire kiluba hemba-français, français-kiluba hemba. Bruxelles: Ministère des Colonies. Introduction, §V, p. 11.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (page headed '— 11 —', section 'V.', signed 'Joseph Vandermeiren, des Missionnaires d'Afrique (Pères Blancs)'). The quoted passage is on the page scan word for word: 'L'accent tonique joue un rôle important en kiluba hemba. En le déplaçant, on s'expose à ne pas être compris ou à dire des choses tout autres que celles qu'on voulait dire, car certains mots, en tout semblables pour l'orthographe, ont des sens totalement différents d'après la place qu'on donne à l'accent tonique. Bien plus, il arrive très souvent qu'un mot, écrit de la même manière et portant le même accent tonique, diffère, quant au sens, suivant que la voyelle de la syllabe est longue ou brève. L'usage certes devra êtr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed stress position is given. The 'accent tonique' of Kiluba-hemba is lexically placed and distinctive: its position alone separates otherwise identical words, and vowel length is a second independent contrast. Colle (1913, tome II p. 661), the companion first-hand source, makes the phonetic nature explicit: every word carries an accent that 'is not the prosodic accent but the tonic, musical or acute accent', i.e. a raised pitch, and in trisyllables this high pitch falls either on the penult or on the antepenult depending on the word (lùbuzi 'big goat', bàluba vs kamùntu 'little man'), 'likewise for shorter and longer words'. Read together: Hemba is a tone (pitch accent-like) language whose word 'accent' is a lexically unpredictable high pitch, not a dynamic stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; Colle says the same holds for shorter and longer words. Vandermeiren adds that vowel length (long vs short, marked grave vs acute in the dictionary) independently distinguishes words that bear the same accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: Vandermeiren gives 'à chaque mot.. son accent tonique' (dictionary citation forms, accent marked with acute on short vowels and grave on long vowels); Colle: 'Chaque mot comporte un accent'. Colle's second-hand-free supporting quote (tome II, p. 661, file): 'Chaque mot comporte un accent, qui n'est pas l'accent prosodique, mais l'accent tonique, musical, ou aigu. Ces trois derniers mots désignent cette même inflexion élevée (le do aigu). Voici un mot de trois syllabes; il possède deux sons graves et un son aigu; le son aigu frappe soit la pénultième, soit l'antipénultième; on dira, par exemple : lùbuzi (une grande chèvre), bàluba, avec l'accent aigu sur lù et sur bà; ou bien kamùntu (un petit homme), avec l'accent aigu sur mù.' The 1912 grammar (not opened) presumably has the fuller treatment.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the Kiluba-hemba of the 'Baluba de l'est' / Baluba-Hemba of the Urua (Buluba-hemba) between the Lualaba and Lake Tanganyika (White Fathers' mission area, Kongolo–Kiambi), i.e. Hemba proper (hemb1242, Guthrie L.34), not Yazi or Zeela; the example forms show the Hemba h-reflex (kihona 'chair', ha-nzibo 'at the house') where Luba-Katanga has p. Vandermeiren's 1913 dictionary and 1912 grammar are the works Glottolog cites for hemb1242; Colle's monograph is the ethnography of the same population and defers to Vandermeiren for the language.

new_statements.quote: 39. L'accent tonique joue un rôle important en kiluba-hemba. En le déplaçant, on s'expose à ne pas être compris ou à dire des choses tout autres que celles qu'on voulait dire. Car certains mots, en tout semblables pour l'orthographe, ont des sens totalement différents d'après la place qu'on donne à l'accent tonique. Ex. : kukùla, racheter de l'esclavage; kúkula, avancer en âge; kutùka, descendre; kútuka, insulter. 40. Il est difficile de former des règles fixes concernant la place de l'accent tonique. L'usage devra servir de guide. [...] 51. Huitième règle. Les verbes à radical dissyllabique ont ordinairement l'accent tonique sur l'avant-dernière syllabe.
new_statements.translation: 39. The tonic accent plays an important role in Kiluba-Hemba. By displacing it one risks not being understood or saying things quite different from what one meant. For certain words, entirely alike in spelling, have totally different meanings according to the place given to the tonic accent. Ex.: kukùla 'redeem from slavery', kúkula 'advance in age'; kutùka 'descend', kútuka 'insult'. 40. It is difficult to form fixed rules about the place of the tonic accent. Usage must serve as guide. [...] 51. Eighth rule. Verbs with a disyllabic root ordinarily have the tonic accent on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Vandermeiren, J. (1912). Grammaire de la langue kiluba-hemba, telle qu'elle est parlée par les Baluba de l'est (Katanga). Bruxelles: Ministère des Colonies. 302 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author, same statement as the catalog's existing entry (Vocabulaire 1913, Introduction §V p. 11 reproduces §39 of the 1912 grammar almost verbatim: contrastive 'accent tonique', minimal pairs by accent place). The grammar adds the full placement chapter: eleven rules (prefix vs root-initial by root length and word class, NC-cluster and contraction length effects, enclitic attraction, reduplication), a secondary accent in quadrisyllables, phrase-level accent shift, tense-particle accent (p. 85) and applicative accent shift (p. 166). Nothing in it contradicts the catalog's 'tone language with a stress statement' reading; the catalog record's empty rule field can now be filled from pp. 17…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The author describes a lexically contrastive 'accent tonique' with minimal pairs (kukùla/kúkula, kutúka/kútuka, kukóma/kúkoma, kufúla/kúfula, kusóka/kúsoka) and says its place follows no fixed rule; he then gives eleven tendencies (pp. 19-22): (1) a vowel from contraction is long but not necessarily accented; (2) a vowel before two consonants (NC) is long and, if it is the last such in the word, ordinarily carries the accent, unless the cluster is followed by a contracted long vowel, which then takes it (kusangêla); (3) an enclitic pronoun pulls the accent onto the syllable immediately before it (séla > selá-kyo); (4) reduplicated roots carry an accent on each copy; (5) inflected words with a monosyllabic root accent the class/concord prefix or infinitive ku- (lífu, kúlya); (6) invariable monosyllables are unaccented unless before an NC-initial word; (7) invariable words with disyllabic root: penult (bíne, héhi); (8) verbs with disyllabic root: ordinarily penult = root-initial (kufúta), except verbs in -uma/-una/-oma/-ona which prefer the accent on ku- (kúmona, kútoma); (9) nouns/adjectives with disyllabic root: ordinarily on the class prefix (mútima, múkazi, lízina), prefixless NC-initial disyllables ('mpuku, 'nzibo) have 'properly speaking no accent' unless the penult vowel is followed by NC (mfíndi, ntámbo); (10) trisyllabic roots: antepenult = root-initial (kulásula) unless an earlier rule dominates; (11) quadrisyllabic words: main accent on the first root syllable plus a second accent on the penult. In connected speech the accent can move (kúlya > kulyá nsima). In modern terms this contrastive, morphologically distributed 'accent' is a pre-tonological description of lexical high tone (the chapter is headed 'Observations sur les tons'); read literally as stress it would be lexical/morphological with weight (NC, contraction length) effects, not a fixed position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §54 p. 22: quadrisyllabic words have, besides the main ('principal ou tonique') accent on the first root syllable, a second accent on the penult (kusótolóla, kuvúngulúla, kusíntakánya); exception: quadrisyllabic verbs derived from a simple verb accented on ku- keep the main accent on ku- and the second accent moves to the antepenult (kúfumúnuna, kúkutúlula). §41 p. 18: a word may have several long syllables 'on which the voice rests' but ordinarily only one carries the accent, except reduplicated words (§47: accent repeated on each copy, lémbalémba, kambalámbalá).
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs in -uma/-una/-oma/-ona accent the prefix ku- (kúmona, kúkuna, kúfuma, kútoma) rather than the root; prefixless NC-initial disyllabic nouns have no accent proper ('mpuku, 'ngolo, 'nzibo; accent appears on an added prefix: bá-mpuku) except when the penult vowel precedes NC (mfíndi, ntámbo, nsímba); invariable monosyllables unaccented except before NC-initial words (i ná mfumu); enclitic object pronouns attract the accent to the preceding syllable (selá-kyo, hitá-ko); connected speech shifts the accent (kutahá ntaho for kutáha, kulyá nsima for kúlya, kuatá nkuni for kuáta); §173 p. 85: some disyllabic verbs carry the accent on the past particle bá (tubá-tibe, tubá-mone); p. 166: in the applicative past the accent moves to the contracted syllable, and in applicatives built on contracted state-pasts it moves to the antepenult; §55 p. 23: from then on acute marks accent on a short vowel, grave on a long vowel, since words with the same accent place can still differ in meaning by vowel length.
new_statements.identity_note: Vandermeiren describes 'la langue kiluba-hemba.. parlée par les Baluba de l'est (Katanga)', written at the White Fathers' mission Lukulu Sacré-Coeur (dated 26 Jan 1910), for the area bounded by the Lukuga to its confluence with the Lualaba (N), the Mrumbi/Mugila mountains and the west shore of Lake Moero (E), a line from the lake to the Lomami (S), and the Lomami up to Moadi then Katompe-Mbuli (W/NW) (Introduction p. 5). Glottolog files this grammar under hemb1242 Hemba; the variety is the eastern 'Kiluba-Hemba' of the Baluba-Hemba (Bantu L.34 area bordering Luba-Katanga L.33), not the Hemba of the Kongolo/Nyunzu north sometimes distinguished from it. He notes minor sub-dialect variation only in passing (e.g. n+i pronounced nyi 'par certaines populations', p. 17).
